                 Abstract
                 Malaysia has pledged to reduce the intensity of Green House Gas (GHG) emission by 45% based on Gross
                 Production Product (GDP) in 2030 and ultimately net-zero carbon emission in 2050 during UNFCCC-COP
                 26 in Scotland. However, the growing energy demands need some of the high contaminant (CO2) natural
                 gas fields in the region to be developed. To mitigate the negative climatic impact of such developments
                 and manage the huge quantities of produced CO2, Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) is the only viable
                 technology in the current world. In this paper, a multidisciplinary subsurface study is conducted to unlock
                 the potential containment for CO2 storage and estimate the effective volume in deep saline aquifer.
                    A fit for purpose 3D geological model was built for K reservoir in Z field. A range of porosity was
                 tabulated from well log data and permeability was estimated from available poro-perm cross plot. Then,
                 a compositional dynamic model with appropriate CO2 storage features is established using CMG-GEM
                 simulator. The initial formation pressure and temperature were estimated from available well tests, and PVT
                 and SCAL data are considered from an analogue field. The base case model was initialized, and several
                 scenarios were run to estimate the optimum effective CO2 storage capacity for injection period of 25 years.
                    The CO2 gas injection started on the January 2025 with 60 MMscf/d injection rate and maximum water
                 withdrawal was set at 30 kbbl/d. The prediction ran until 2050. An effective CO2 storage capacity for non-
                 voidage case is estimated at 4.9 Bscf for a commingled injector with no producer case. This contributed
                 only 3% of the theoretical storage capacity that can be sequestered due to high pressure build-up in the
                 reservoir. For voidage case, one injector and one producer (commingled) case predicted to effectively
                 sequestered 80.13 Bscf, which is approximately 51% of the total theoretical storage capacity. The simulation
                 was further optimized with two injector and one producer (commingled) case where a total of 95.44 Bscf
                 gas is predicted to be sequestered in the reservoir. This contributed to the highest effective CO2 storage
                 volume, approximately at 61% of the total theoretical storage capacity.
                    This study presents the feasibility and optimization of CO2 sequestration in saline aquifer zone for one
                 of Malaysia pre-development fields that can be as part of forecasting the CO2 injectivity and behaviour
                 in storage reservoir during containment. Based on the study outcomes, it was well understood that the
                 small, restricted saline aquifers may not present the greatest avenue for sustainable and economic CO2

                 Introduction
                 Re-screening study on drilled dry structures in Malay Basin was carried-out during FY2021 as part of
                 PETRONAS's initiatives to identify saline aquifer candidates for feasibility study and broaden the funnel
                 of CO2 storage sites in Peninsular Malaysia. A total of 34 candidates were ranked and shortlisted based
                 on the evaluation of critical storage elements which are the reservoir, seal presence & effectiveness, and
                 trap presence. This re-screening exercise was carried out utilizing the available information for saline
                 aquifer study, well logs, exploration interpretation and other available reports. As results, six potential
                 candidates with individual field's theoretical storage capacity ranging between 0.5-23 Tscf and four fields
                 were identified with mid to high chance of feasibility with individual field's storage capacity ranging
                 between ∼0.05 to 4.6 Tscf. On top of that, the study also identified opportunities from X, Y and Z field
                 with theoretical storage capacity ranging between ∼1.1 to 1.8 Tscf.
                    The integrated subsurface study was conducted for containment assessment of X, Y and Z fields.
                 High level containment analysis included reservoir characterization, reservoir correlation, sedimentology,
                 structural configuration and well integrity analysis. The study concluded that two out of the three studied
                 structures (X and Y fields) were assessed to be associated with high trap risk or no trap and hence were
                 not analysed further for storage capacity assessment. Similarly, it was found that the J and L reservoirs
                 in Z field were also found have no trap presence and not feasible for CO2 storage. Only the K reservoirs
                 in Z field fulfilled all the criteria of storage screening parameters and were selected as potential storage
                 candidate for capacity estimation.
                    The exploration well, Z-1 was spudded on 17 September 2010 and reached TD at depth 3142m MDDF/
                 2736 m TVDSS on 23 October 2010. It penetrated 418 m (MD) into the fractured metamorphic reservoir.
                 Minor oil and gas were discovered in both K7.1 Sand and L1 Sand, which was the secondary objective.
                 However, there was no hydrocarbon shows in the primary objective of the well which is the fractured
                 metamorphic reservoir. Hydrocarbon type in K7.1 was proven by sample taken from MDT-IFA logging run.
                 L1 Sand was interpreted as oil bearing formation from the petrophysical analysis. Static Gradient Survey
                 (SGS) was conducted during testing and suggested that L2 Sand is a water bearing formation. MDT Dual
                 Packer was conducted in K5 Sand and the fluid type on surface confirmed that K5 Sand is a water bearing
                 formation.
                    Based on the post drill analysis (PDA), the petroleum system elements in Z field are classified as proven
                 & effective in K & L reservoirs resulted from the HC accumulation in the reservoirs (Table 1). The potential
                 reservoir zone for Z field Storage, J, K & L reservoir been selected. Based on analysis, reservoirs J & K
                 selected as the best potential zones for storage in Z field whereas L reservoir been excluded due to limited
                 net reservoir thickness in that zone (Table 2).

                 Effective Storage Capacity Estimation
                 The workflow of the modelling work applied in this project is shown in Figure 3. The modelling workflow
                 started with 3-D static model construction from geologist. Geologist has constructed a high level 3-D model
                 in Petrel to define the average porosity, permeability, net to gross, water saturation and other parameters
                 utilizing available data in Z field. The average properties from available RESSUM have been incorporated
                 into the model. The high-level static 3-D model has total number of 318,750 grid cells with 100m × 100m
                 grid dimension and covered Z field structure only from Top J layer to Top L shale layer. In terms of
                 volumetric, geologist has incorporated a region known as ‘Region 1’ to calculate the bulk volume, net
                 volume and pore volume that represented the Z field structure for this study.

                                                                       Figure 3—The storage capacity assessment workflow


                    The high-level static model was then passed to reservoir engineers in .bin format and exported into CMG
                 software as reference model. In this study, CMG-GEM (version 2020.10) was used as a compositional
                 simulator for CO2 storage capacity assessment, injectivity and sensitivity analysis. Upon receiving the static
                 model, the model was verified before performing the model initialization. The permeability data is estimated
                 from nearby field. Porosity and permeability values are different for every layer in Z field but there will be
                 only one value of porosity and permeability applied to each of the layers which are in this case, the average
                 porosity and average permeability as input. Laterally, those layers will be like homogenous layer.
                    Next, the initial model condition such as datum depth, pressure at datum depth and water-gas contact in
                 the model were defined. The formation pressure is calculated by water gradient of 0.433 psi/ft at specified
                 mid-depth for every layers. In terms of PVT, typical PVT of gas (C1+CO2) is used for modelling and same
                 PVT have been used for all layers.
                    After proper model initialization, the model is run with few scenarios case of commingled CO2 injectors
                 with and without water producer for a period of 25 years. Some constraints have been applied to CO2
                 injectors such as maximum bottom hole pressure based on geomechanics analysis and maximum gas
                 injection rate. The impact of introducing water producer is significant and allowing more spaces for CO2 to
                 occupy the reservoirs. The base case is further optimized to maximize the potential CO2 storage capacity.
                 Lastly, effective CO2 storage volume is estimated based on cumulative CO2 gas injection for each layer at
                 the end of injection period and compared against theoretical storage capacity.

                 Modelling Results

                 One Commingled Injector (No Producer)
                 One commingled injector with no produced is placed at the edge of the Z field reservoir model as shown
                 in Figure 5 to mimic a non-voidage case model. A maximum of 60 MMscf/d of pure CO2 gas is set to
                 be injected and the maximum bottomhole pressure is set at 5000 psi. However, due to the initial pressure
                 build-up in the reservoir, the injector was shut after 200 days of injection period. The effective storage
                 gas capacity is estimated at 4.9 Bscf at the end of the simulation run. This contributes to the 3% of the
                 theoretical storage capacity that can be sequestered. Figure 6 and Figure 7 shows the gas injection profile
                 as well as average reservoir pressure for non-voidage case model, respectively. Clearly, for non-voidage
                 case, the maximum geo-mechanical pressure limit has been reached. Thus, this scenario is not a suitable
                 candidate for CO2 storage in Z field.

                    In summary, the highest effective CO2 storage volume is identified approximately 95.44 Bscf as optimized
                 case, which is estimated around 61% of the theoretical storage volume, 157.03 Bscf. Based on this study
                 outcomes, technically, it is not recommended to proceed further with CO2 injection planning in Z field due
                 to very small effective storage volume estimation and high uncertainties from the dynamc modelling inputs
                 as of this study.

                 Conclusion
                 The dynamic simulation scenarios demonstrated the fact that the effective CO2 storage capacity for restricted
                 saline aquifers can be significantly enhanced by creating voidage or pressure sink by production of formation
                 water. CCS is crucial for the timely development of high contaminant gas fields in the PM area and
                 saline aquifers are expected to play a vital role in managing the GHG emissions associated with the
                 development of high contaminant gas fields. However, during the current study it was well understood that
                 the small, restricted saline aquifers may not present the greatest avenue for sustainable and economic CO2
                 sequestration due to their limited size and the requirement of water production to create additional voidage/
                 pressure sink. In such a scenario, extensive and open aquifer systems in the region may be analyzed for
                 their containment integrity and effective storage capacities.
